cohort_measured_fresh.note: The recorded backlog said 'MA 422'. Re-measured rather than inherited. The two defects fixed here cut ACROSS source classes, so neither the old number nor any single class is the unit.

defect_1_default_chairs.finding: The row concedes there is no evidence and seats the middle anyway: "Not tracked by Act on Mass. No immigration legislation found in sponsored bills. Moderate Democrat default." A CENTRE CHAIR IS A CLAIM, NOT A DEFAULT -- chair 3 is shown to voters as this person's position, and the corpus already has a way of saying unknown: value 0.
defect_1_default_chairs.the_wider_class: 106 MA rows reason from a NON-SPONSORSHIP or from absence in a third-party tracker. AN ABSENT SIGNATURE IS NOT A VOTE AGAINST. Only the self-condemning subset -- the rows that actually say "default" or "insufficient evidence" -- was written here, because that needs no judgement call. The other 67 are recorded and owed a reading.
defect_1_default_chairs.false_positive_excluded: Sal N. DiDomenico / judicial-transparency uses "a default-to-openness philosophy" in the opposite sense and cites real bills (S.1066, S.1068). Not a defect.

defect_2_h4264_cluster.finding: 39 rows cite malegislature.gov/Bills/192/H4264 as "the Massachusetts climate roadmap" or "the Environmental Justice Policy Act". H.4264 OF THE 192nd IS "An Act establishing a year-round market rate rental housing trust in the town of Truro".
defect_2_h4264_cluster.the_number_is_right_for_a_different_cour: H.4264 of the 191st IS "An Act relative to environmental justice in the commonwealth". MA renumbers every General Court exactly as Maryland renumbers every session -- the hazard that nearly produced a mass false finding in migration 1898. Every cited number was resolved in the court its URL names AND in every other court before any verdict. The real climate roadmap is S.9 of the 192nd, which this corpus cites correctly on 21 other rows.

five_verdicts_not_one.NOT_DISTINCTIVE (28, blanked): Claim support for the roadmap. S.9 passed the House 144-14 and the Senate 39-1. A near-unanimous vote cannot establish a DISTINCTIVE position (Newhouse 385-41, mig 1894; Dingell 417-10, mig 1896). 91% of the House voted the same way.
five_verdicts_not_one.ROLLCALL_REPAIR (3, repaired, chair unch: Berthiaume, McKenna and Frost say they voted AGAINST it, and the roll call confirms it. THE CONVERSE OF THE LEHMAN RULE: dissent from a 91% majority IS distinctive -- 14 of 158. Citation repaired to S.9 + the roll call; chair 4 kept after comparing the rung text.
five_verdicts_not_one.INVERTED_VOTE (1, blanked): Colleen M. Garry's row says she "voted for the 2021 climate roadmap bill". SHE VOTED NAY -- she is one of the fourteen. Retiring on the citation alone would have been right for the wrong reason; trusting it would have left an inverted chair standing.
five_verdicts_not_one.TRUE_BUT_LADDER_SCOPE (3, blanked, claim: Madaro, Tyler and Holmes ARE on the 87-name Cosponsors page of H.4264/191 (Madaro first, as an original petitioner). But the bill DIED ("No further action taken", 1/5/2021) so it was never "signed into law", and Season 2 rewrote local-environment rung 1 from "require green space, tree preservation and environmental review" to "make environmental protection the overriding priority -- block or sharply limit development". Co-sponsoring a cumulative-impact review bill is not evidence of blocking development. The Carson call of migration 1896; for the ladder-scope register. The verified fact is written into the blank.
five_verdicts_not_one.NOT_A_COSPONSOR (1, blanked): David Biele served in the 191st but is NOT among the 87. A checked absence.
five_verdicts_not_one.NOT_SERVING (3, blanked): Giannino (from the 192nd), Garcia and Montaño (from the 193rd) were NOT IN THE LEGISLATURE when H.4264/191 existed. The claim is IMPOSSIBLE, not merely unsupported. CHECK TENURE BEFORE READING A SPONSORSHIP OR A NON-VOTE.

defect_2_h4264_cluster.roll_call_parse_is_asymmetric: The PDF is a four-column grid that pdftotext splits mid-cell, so continuation names lose their marker. The 14 NAYS parse cleanly and were verified against the roll call's OWN declared total of 14 before any name was used. The YEA parse recovers only 39 of 144, so NOTHING is asserted from it: this migration proves someone voted Nay, never that someone voted Yea. Every claim in the migration respects that limit.

blocked.running_total_unfixable: migs 1896 (3) + 1897 (3) + 1898 (20) + 1899 (4) = 30 defective chairs unfixable because `immigration` has no Season 2 pin.

not_fixed_recorded.the_676_bill_sweep: A sweep of every one of the 676 distinct bills this cohort cites -- "does the cited bill say what the row says it says?" -- was still running when this migration was cut. The H.4264 cluster is ONE bill out of 676, found only because it was the most-cited (39 rows). The sweep is the way to find the rest and is the next step. Method and cache are in the scratchpad; the key rule is to resolve a number in EVERY court before calling it wrong.
not_fixed_recorded.the_232_profile_only_keys: Need the per-court Sponsored/Cosponsored lists the way migration 1898 read Maryland's (/Legislators/Profile/<code>/<court>/Bills/Sponsored). Untouched here.
not_fixed_recorded.act_on_mass_uncited: 147 MA rows name "Act on Mass" as their evidence; 20 of them do not cite it as a source at all. Uncited evidence, recorded.

rows.original_reasoning: Madaro authored and championed the Massachusetts Environmental Justice Policy Act (H.4264/S.2820), signed into law in 2021, which requires state agencies to consider disproportionate environmental burdens on low-income communities of color. East Boston — his district — is a designated Environmental Justice community facing air quality impacts from Logan Airport, the highway system, and industrial facilities. He has been the Legislature's leading voice on environmental justice.

Murray supported the Massachusetts climate roadmap legislation (H.4264, 2021) which set binding emissions reductions targets and expanded offshore wind procurement. He has backed clean energy transition legislation in the 194th General Court consistent with the MA Democratic caucus position on climate action.

Ayers voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported clean energy legislation and offshore wind investment. His coastal South Shore district is particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts. His record reflects mainstream Democratic support for state climate goals.

Tyler co-sponsored the Environmental Justice Policy Act (H.4264) and has been among its strongest advocates in the House. Roxbury is a designated EJ community with elevated air pollution from I-93 and Route 1. She has championed green infrastructure investment, urban heat island mitigation, and air quality improvements specifically for EJ communities of color.

Garry voted for the 2021 climate roadmap bill overall but has a more moderate record on aggressive climate mandates than her Cambridge and Somerville colleagues. Her Merrimack Valley district has concerns about energy costs and manufacturing impacts of rapid climate policy changes. Her record reflects a balanced approach supporting climate goals while being cautious about economic impacts on her district.

Donahue supported the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) and clean energy legislation in the 194th General Court. He has backed climate action and clean energy transition consistent with the MA Democratic caucus, supporting reduced emissions and renewable energy development for Worcester and central Massachusetts.

LeBoeuf has been an active advocate for aggressive climate action in the MA House, supporting the 2021 climate roadmap (H.4264) and clean energy legislation. He co-sponsored bills calling for even more aggressive emissions reductions and has been among the more vocal climate advocates in the legislature, backing clean energy investment for Worcester and central Massachusetts.

Biele co-sponsored environmental justice legislation including H.4264 protections for communities of color facing disproportionate pollution. Chinatown — the densest part of his district — is a designated Environmental Justice community surrounded by highway infrastructure (Mass Pike, I-93) and faces significant air quality burdens. He has been an advocate for reducing highway pollution impacts and investing in urban green infrastructure.

Muradian voted against the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) as part of the Republican minority opposing binding emissions reduction mandates. He has expressed concerns about the economic impact of aggressive climate legislation on businesses and residents in his suburban Worcester County district.

Berthiaume voted against the Massachusetts climate roadmap legislation (H.4264, 2021) as part of the Republican minority that opposed binding emissions reduction mandates and accelerated clean energy timelines. He has expressed concerns about the economic costs of aggressive climate legislation on working families and businesses in his rural district.

O'Day supported the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) and clean energy legislation in the 194th General Court. He has backed climate action and clean energy transition consistent with the MA Democratic caucus, supporting reduced emissions and renewable energy development.

Murphy voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. His coastal South Shore district gives him particular awareness of climate impacts including sea-level rise and storm surge. He supports the state's climate framework while being attentive to economic impacts on working-class constituents.

Giannino co-sponsored the Environmental Justice Policy Act (H.4264) and has advocated for air quality improvements in East Boston. Her district faces elevated particulate matter and noise pollution from Logan Airport operations, and she has been an active voice for addressing these environmental burdens on her predominantly immigrant community.

Mahoney supported the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) and clean energy legislation in the 194th General Court. He has backed climate action and clean energy transition consistent with the MA Democratic caucus position, supporting renewable energy development for Worcester and central Massachusetts.

Marsi voted against the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) as part of the Republican minority opposing binding emissions reduction mandates and accelerated clean energy timelines. He has expressed concerns about economic costs to rural communities and businesses from aggressive climate regulations.

Zlotnik co-sponsored the 2021 Massachusetts climate roadmap legislation (H.4264) that set binding emissions reductions targets and expanded offshore wind procurement. He has supported clean energy transition bills in the 194th General Court, indicating strong support for state-level climate action consistent with the Massachusetts Democratic caucus position.

McKenna voted against the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) as part of the Republican minority opposing binding emissions reduction mandates. He has raised concerns about economic costs of aggressive climate legislation on businesses and residents in his rural southern Worcester County district.

McGonagle voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap bill committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported offshore wind investment and clean energy legislation. His record on climate is moderate-supportive: he backs the mainstream MA climate framework but is less vocal on aggressive phase-out measures.

Garcia co-sponsored the Environmental Justice Policy Act (H.4264) and has been among its most passionate advocates. Chelsea is the state's most densely populated city and has long served as a sacrifice zone for industrial and fossil fuel infrastructure. She has championed air quality monitoring, GreenWave clean energy incentives for EJ communities, and phasing out the Chelsea Creek fuel terminal.

Donaghue has been a notable advocate for climate action in the MA House, serving on environmental committees and actively supporting the 2021 climate roadmap (H.4264) and subsequent clean energy legislation. She has been among the more vocal champions of offshore wind, clean energy transition, and aggressive emissions reductions, and has authored or co-sponsored climate-related legislation in the 194th General Court.

Lipper-Garabedian voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. She has supported clean energy investment and building efficiency programs. Her record shows consistent Democratic support for the state's climate framework.

Decker co-sponsored the 100% Renewable Energy Act and voted in favor of the 2021 climate roadmap bill (H.4264) committing Massachusetts to net-zero emissions by 2050. She has consistently supported offshore wind investment, clean energy incentives, and legislation to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels. Her district includes environmentally active Cambridge residents and she has attended climate advocacy events hosted by 350 Massachusetts.

Decker supported the MBTA Communities zoning reform requiring denser housing near transit stations, reflecting support for increased density in urban areas. However, she has also championed tenant protections and community input in planning decisions, balancing density goals with displacement prevention. Her position favors more housing production in transit-oriented locations combined with strong affordability requirements.

Cusack voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported clean energy investment and offshore wind development. His South Shore coastal district is vulnerable to climate impacts and he has backed the state's climate goals while being attentive to constituent concerns about energy costs.

Kilcoyne supported the Massachusetts climate roadmap (H.4264, 2021) and clean energy legislation in the 194th General Court. Soter voted against the Massachusetts climate roadmap legislation (H.4264, 2021) as part of the Republican minority opposing binding emissions reduction mandates and accelerated clean energy requirements. Day voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported clean energy investment and building efficiency programs. His record reflects mainstream Democratic support for state climate goals.

Haggerty voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing the state to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported clean energy investment, offshore wind, and building efficiency programs. His votes reflect mainstream Democratic support for the state's climate framework.

Speaker Mariano moved the 2021 MA climate roadmap bill through the House and it passed under his leadership, committing Massachusetts to net-zero emissions by 2050. However, he has been more cautious than climate activists on aggressive mandates, preferring a balanced approach sensitive to ratepayer and business impacts. He supports clean energy investment but is not the lead champion for the most ambitious climate proposals.

Holmes co-sponsored the Environmental Justice Policy Act (H.4264) and has been a champion of linking environmental justice to racial equity in Mattapan. His district is surrounded by highways and industrial zones generating disproportionate pollution burdens. He has advocated for urban tree canopy expansion, urban agriculture, and green infrastructure investment to improve environmental quality in his community.

Montaño co-sponsored the Environmental Justice Policy Act (H.4264) and has been an advocate for linking environmental protection to racial equity in Mission Hill. Her district contains EJ communities affected by highway pollution from Route 9 and adjacent industrial zones. She has championed green infrastructure and air quality improvement investments in underserved communities.

His suburban district contains significant conservation land and his record shows consistent support for environmental protection.

Ultrino voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap bill committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported clean energy investment and building efficiency programs. His record reflects mainstream Democratic support for state climate policy.

Galvin voted for the 2021 MA climate roadmap committing to net-zero emissions by 2050. He has supported clean energy investment and offshore wind development. His record reflects mainstream Democratic support for state climate goals.
